name: Cooperatives & Local Food Systems

objectives.text: Describe how a farmers market connects local growers with local buyers
Identify local food outlets in the community, such as farmers markets, farm stands, CSAs, and farm-to-school programs
Trace the path of a food product from farm to table in a local supply chain and in a long-distance supply chain
Explain how an agricultural cooperative allows farmers to work together to buy supplies or sell products
Compare the price of a food product at a farmers market and at a grocery store and explain reasons for the difference
Classify examples of agricultural cooperatives as marketing, supply, service, or credit cooperatives
Explain how a community supported agriculture program shares production risk and reward between farmers and members
Explain the cooperative principles of user ownership, user control, and user benefit, including one member one vote
Compare the structure of a cooperative to that of a corporation, including ownership, voting control, and distribution of profits
Describe the roles of members, the board of directors, and hired management in governing an agricultural cooperative
Summarize the consumer trends and market demands that drive the local food movement
Calculate patronage refunds for cooperative members using net margins and each member's volume of business
Interpret USDA data on agricultural cooperative membership and sales and on local food sales
Explain the food safety and regulatory requirements, such as GAP certification and cottage food laws, that apply to selling farm products locally
Compare direct-to-consumer and intermediated local food channels, such as CSAs, food hubs, restaurants, and institutions, and assess how market demand shapes each
Analyze the role of cooperatives and local food systems in supporting rural communities and economies
Analyze the business plan of an agricultural cooperative, including capitalization through member equity, retained patronage, and borrowed capital
Evaluate the benefits and challenges of joining an agricultural cooperative for a given farm operation
Evaluate the environmental and economic tradeoffs of short supply chains compared with conventional food distribution
Propose a distribution plan that moves an SAE product through a local food channel to meet a specific market demand
Develop a proposal for a community local food system initiative, such as a cooperative, food hub, or farm-to-school program

changes: Kept all six original objectives, rewording the co-op versus corporation comparison to name voting control, and anchored the upper-grade ones to fitting AFNR codes. Added competencies the old template missed: identifying local food outlets, tracing local versus long-distance supply chains, comparing market prices, classifying cooperative types, CSA risk sharing, cooperative principles, governance roles, patronage refund calculation, interpreting USDA cooperative and local food data, local sales regulations such as GAP and cottage food laws, comparing local distribution channels, analyzing cooperative capitalization, evaluating short supply chain tradeoffs, and an SAE local distribution plan. General ownership structures, starting a business, and careers were left to the sibling sub-topics.
